Giga Photo Award: Stories on the Impact of Connectivity

This gallery features the winning images of the 2026 Giga Photo Award. The photos may be used for UNICEF advocacy purposes. For any other use externally, please contact UNICEF for permission.

column2: Caption

Title: Sudan
Photographer: Faiz Abubakr Mohamed

Caption: 
In 2025, prolonged power outages plunged Omdurman into darkness. Electricity failed for days at a time, cutting access to news and communication across the city.

This story follows Ammar, who runs a small online news channel during the blackouts. On rooftops and street corners, he searched for fragile signals, walking long distances or waiting through the night to upload updates. As connectivity disappeared, people relied on him to know what was happening in Sudan.

Working by the faint glow of his phone, Ammar documented fear, resilience, and daily survival. In a city without power, information became light. Not in the streets, but in the act of telling the story.


Location:  Sudan

Title: A Completely Normal Day
Photographer: Antti Yrjönen

Caption: 
Olena Mykhailivna Loboda, a mathematics teacher in Chernihiv, northern Ukraine, teaches an online class in 2025 as security risks and air-raid alerts force schools to switch between classroom and remote learning.

 “This is a completely normal day,” she says. “Some pupils can get online, others have a weak connection. We share the materials and help them catch up.”

Location: Ukraine

Title: Inside prison - “The Phone Is Everything” 
Photographer: Magali Druscovich

Location: Argentina

Project Description: 

In 2020, pandemic lockdowns cut prisons off from the outside world. In Argentina, visits stopped, and programs ended, until an exceptional court decision allowed mobile phone use in Buenos Aires’ provincial prisons.

This project follows Paola, serving a four-year sentence in Penitentiary Unit 47, and other women navigating that shift. 

Phones became essential tools to maintain family ties, continue education, and sustain a sense of self beyond incarceration.

Connectivity does not remove the walls, but inside Unit 47 it reduced isolation, strengthened support networks, and opened a bridge toward life after release.

Title: Energy Paradox
Photographer: Francis Ogunyemi

Location:  Nigeria 

Project Description:

This project documents everyday life in Ijebu Igbo, a semi-urban community two hours from Lagos, seen through the perspective of an indigene.

As unreliable public power persists, solar energy and improvised charging solutions increasingly shape how people live and work. Across homes, streets, and small businesses, access to electricity determines participation in the digital world, where communication, commerce, and family ties depend on mobile devices.

The project focuses on ordinary moments shaped by the search for power: charging a phone, keeping a business running, staying connected. Rather than technology itself, the work centers the human experience of improvisation, resilience, and uncertainty in a place where connection to the wider world remains both essential and fragile.


Caption: 

A high-angle view of Ijebu Igbo, an ancient Yoruba town approximately two hours drive from Lagos. It reveals a town in the midst of an energy transition. Solar panels sit atop rusted roofs just meters away from petrol-powered generators and a semi-active fueling station, illustrating the overlapping and often conflicting layers of Nigeria’s energy landscape. Ijebu Igbo, October 3, 2024.

Caption: 

A communal charging outlet serves as a vital piece of modern infrastructure. This "digital altar" is where residents gather not just to power their devices, but to ensure their continued participation in a world that requires them to be "always on," even when the power is off. These charging outlets are a popular business venture in the town which people often combine with their other businesses. People get to charge as low as 100 to 200 Nigerian Naira, depending on the type of device. Igbaire, Ijebu Igbo, October 1, 2024.

Caption: 

Mary Olakiitan, 35, poses for a portrait inside her local chemist shop, while her husband, Adewale is engrossed with his phone on the night of 25th September, 2024. For most business owners like Mary, they rely heavily on solar to light up their workspace at night, keep phones charged for transactions and to get things running. For Mary and her husband, the mobile device is a silent partner whose utility is entirely dependent on the successful, daily search for a reliable charge. September 25, 2024

Caption: 

At night, the illuminated sign of a communications shop stands as a glowing gateway. In a community like Ijebu Igbo where traditional power is critically unstable, these hubs of repair and accessory sales are the essential mechanics of connectivity, they offer varying services that keep the town's digital heartbeat steady. October 1, 2024

Caption: 

Alowonle Mustapha, 44, a farmer, interacts with a compact, wall-mounted solar charging system. Alowonle resides in a farming settlement in Ijebu Igbo and he's one out of just three persons to own a compact, portable solar system like this in the settlement. The shift to alternative energy is often a personal act of independence, a do-it-yourself endeavour born from the necessity to stay connected to family, work, and the wider world, especially for those that stay a little far from the main town and have no access at all to electricity. Abobi Village, Ijebu Igbo, August 28, 2024

Caption: 

Late evening in the living room of Funke Olanike, 59, a retired headteacher, who now runs a small cement store by her house. Funke sits in her living room, engrossed in her phone, with her godson, Timi, watching the solar powered TV in the background. In 2022, shortly after her retirement, she decided to choose convenience and made an installment purchase of solar powered gadgets and lights for her house. Even when the domestic grid falters, the hunger for news and family connection remains constant, driving a quiet but persistent demand for the energy that keeps the conversation alive. Oke Odo, Ijebu Igbo, August 23, 2024.

Caption: 

Mayowa, 30, a barber, uses the flash light from his phone to complete a client’s haircut during a power outage. His recent transition from wired to rechargeable tools is a quiet but strong act of adaptation. It is a necessary evolution for a small business owner in a landscape where the grid is no longer a constant. Ijebu Igbo. September 25, 2024

Caption: 

A close-up of a solar charging kit strapped to a rough surface wall with a simple rubber band. With its tangled wires and improvised stability, it represents sophisticated global technology powered by the most resourceful, local means. Attached with it is a cellphone. This solar system features three lights with a total output of 480 lumens that can be linked to illuminate multiple rooms, a battery control unit, and a 7 W solar panel. The battery control unit also has one USB port for charging phones. Abobi Village, Ijebu Igbo, August 28, 2024.

Caption: 

Shelves lined with high-capacity power banks represent the commercialisation of the energy crisis. These devices have become essential commodities for people to stay connected. People have grown to rely on portable reservoirs of power, for a community that has learned never to rely solely on the wall socket. August 28, 2024.

Caption: 

Men work together to install new solar panels on a residential roof. This scene reflects the labor-intensive and collective nature of the energy transition. In Ijebu Igbo, only few have the financial capacity to install this kind of intensive solar system for their residential use. Energy access strongly correlates with quality of life and development, which is why the transition to sustainable energy becomes socially complex in many regions, and this indirectly affects digital connectivity. Idode, Ijebu Igbo, December 12, 2024

Caption: ​

A POS service sign glows along a dark street in Oke-odo as a motorcyclist pauses for a transaction. In Nigeria’s digital-first economy, these agents are the essential gatekeepers of financial inclusion, yet their efficiency is fundamentally dependent on the availability of electricity. Here, the speed of commerce is often dictated by the stability of the grid. Oke-odo, Ijebu Igbo. September 2, 2024.

Caption: 

A silhouetted figure stands before a "Be Happy" graffiti tag at a local pepper soup joint. In a landscape of infrastructural uncertainty, the sign serves as both an irony and an anthem; a testament to the resilience of a community that prioritizes connection and joy despite the fragility of the power that sustains it. Ijebu Igbo. September 25, 2024

Title: Internet Cafes
Photographer: Ammar Abubaker

Caption: 
Sudan is now considered one of the largest, if not the largest humanitarian crises in the world. According to UNHCR, over 12 million people have been forcibly displaced since the conflict between the RSF and SAF began on April 15, 2023. More than 3 million of them are now refugees and asylum seekers. The city of Renk in South Sudan has been receiving over 3,000 refugees from Sudan every day. However, Renk has no cellular internet, so people walk 2 kilometers from the UNHCR Transit Centre to the city market, where they can find the so-called "internet cafés", small shops that rent hourly WiFi connections. There, they check daily updates, contact their families, and receive money transfers. In the frame, a group of fellow Sudanese refugees who were using Satellite internet to contact their family, Ms. Fatima (not her real name) on the left sitting beside her daughter while contacting her husband and son who are currently in White Nile State in Sudan and giving them Updates about her asylum registration process. Renk, South Sudan, January 6, 2024


Location: South Sudan

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Location:  France

Project Description:

This long-term project is a tribute to all those, like Donna, who have left everything behind to build a better future for their families. Through her journey, I explore the human cost of exile, but also the resilience it reveals—particularly the invisible threads that bind loved ones across borders. In exile, technology has become a vital lifeline. It allows Donna to remain a mother, a daughter, and a friend—despite the physical separation.

Donna, 47, comes from a remote mountain village in the Philippines. The eldest daughter of farmers, she dreamt of becoming a nurse but left her country to pay for her children’s education. Before arriving in France 13 years ago, she paid a smuggler €13,000. Since then, she has worked full-time for a wealthy Libyan family, sending every euro home. Her sacrifices bore fruit: her eldest daughter, Nicole, is now a qualified nurse. Yet, Donna has not seen her children or parents in over a decade.

Her connection to them survives thanks to smartphones, patchy Wi-Fi, and a routine of voice messages and video calls. Technology allows her to witness birthdays, send lullabies, and offer comfort after a bad school day. These moments—fleeting but essential—are the only form of presence she can offer. I have documented this intimacy from both sides: in France, where Donna works and lives in the shadows, and in the Philippines, where her voice echoes in the family home through a cracked phone screen.

The story also speaks to the broader experience of nearly 10 million overseas Filipino workers, 80% of whom are women. In France alone, nearly 50,000 Filipinas work as domestic helpers, many of them undocumented. They are part of a global chain of care that remains largely unseen, yet sustains entire economies and generations.

Through Donna’s story, I illustrate what sociologist Abdelmalek Sayad called the “double absence”—immigrants are both invisible here and missed there. But technology has carved out a third space: one of digital presence, where love, guidance, and identity still circulate. In this space, exile is not just defined by separation, but by connection.


Caption: 

December 2021. After a hard day's work, Donna, as usual, waits for her children to wake up 10,000 km away so that she can check up on them.The only remedy to try to compensate for this absence is to use other relays, essentially the now ritualized use of the cell phone. Despite the sadness of not being able to be with her, Nicole's success in her studies is a source of great pride for Donna. It allows her to face all the sacrifices she has made and continues to make. Nicole now works as a nurse in a hospital and is able to contribute to the family's expenses as well. This is a great source of hope for Donna.

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: Tublay, Philippines - August 2019. Donna's family lives in a small village in the highlands of Tublay, 3 hours drive from Baguio City, the nearest big city. Gathered on the doorstep of their home, Donna's parents and two of her sons are waiting for her phone call from the Whatsapp video application. This is the only place where there is sufficient internet reception. When Donna's mother sees her daughter, she bursts into tears: only she understands what her daughter is going through because she too had to go into exile in her youth. The children are joking.

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: January 2020. Donna closes the door of her maid's room in the 16th arrondissement of Paris. Once again history repeats itself and she has to leave. She left her employer who rented her this room after he falsely accused her of theft.

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: Tublay, Philippines - August 2019. Donna comes from a poor peasant family that has always lived in this small rural municipality. Donna's parents and sister live in this house where they have been able to do some work thanks to the money Donna sends them. In traditional families in the Philippines, like Donna's, it is common for several generations to live together because they all depend on the same source of income.

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: Donna, 47 years old, comes from a poor peasant family living in a rural village in the mountains 300 km from Manila. Her parents have always cultivated the land. She got married very young and has 4 children. She dreamed of becoming a nurse but went into exile to pay for her children's education. Before arriving in Paris 8 years ago she had to pay a smuggler 13000 euros. When she arrived in Paris, she was working full time for a rich family from the Gulf countries, and in a villa on the French Riviera. She sends all her income for her family and her children's school fees. Today it is her eldest daughter, Nicole, 21 years old, who has managed to get her nursing degree, a great source of pride for Donna. Without papers, she still doesn't know when she'll be able to return to the Philippines. It has been 11 years since she has seen her children and family. Donna now works full-time as a nanny for a French family. Still undocumented, she has an employment contract that will enable her to start a regularization procedure. Little by little, she feels she's gaining independence, even if the slowness of the procedures scares her. And the temptation to take a plane with no return is always present when, for example, her son is not well or her mother has a stroke. She can't imagine her mother dying without ever seeing her again.

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: Tublay, Philippines. August 2019. The three generations of women are gathered at the entrance of their house. Only one absent, Donna. Having obtained her nursing diploma, Nicole dreams of being able to go abroad to practice her profession.

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: Donna takes the metro to work every day. Being undocumented, she's afraid of being stopped and sent to a detention center like a friend of hers. She's always careful to make sure she's in order on urban transport. Here on the Paris metro, a mother with her two children. On the other side of the metro, Donna, who hasn't seen her childrens for 11 years.

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: Tublay, Philippines. August 2019. Nicole, 21, Donna's oldest daughter, and her three brothers spend a lot of time together. They sleep in the same room. Their intensive use of the cell phone not only fills the boredom but also allows them to isolate themselves and compensate a little bit for their lack of privacy.

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: Mars 2020. Saint Ouen . Among friends of the Filipino community, Donna gets a tattoo of her new rank in her fraternity. She is now vice-president of this informal association. The Filipino community organizes itself into fraternities and informal associations to allow members to help each other in case of need. Events" organize the social life, allowing to put money in common, in case of health problems for the families left in the Philippines. This money also makes it possible to repatriate to their native country the bodies of those who die in France.

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: Tublay, Philippines. August 2019. Jon, 45 years old husband of Donna and their four children. Apart from a few irregular assignments as a cab driver, Jon has no job. In a Filipino society that remains very macho (divorce and abortion are forbidden), the husbands of overseas women's are forced to take care of the children while being financially dependent on their wives.

Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: Tublay, Philippines - August 2019. Nicole at the window is bored she can't go out because of the rainy seasonDonna comes from a poor peasant family that has always lived in this small rural municipality. Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: December 2024, Paris. Donna (through the window) is now working full-time as a nanny for a French family in a beautiful district of Paris. Though still undocumented, she has secured an employment contract that enabled her to begin the process of applying for legal residency. But her application for a residence permit was declared incomplete in August 2024. She now has to start the whole procedure all over again. And the temptation to take a one-way flight back home always looms, especially when her son is unwell or her mother suffers a stroke. She can't bear the thought of her mother dying without seeing her again.

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: August 2019. Nicole goes to her university in Baguio City, 3 hours drive from the family home . Here with her brother Russell, after picking up her stuff at her university and trying on the costume she will wear to the graduation ceremony. She gradually adapted to city life.

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: December 2023, Paris. Donna sends 80 percent of her earnings to the Philippines, fulfilling a constant stream of financial needs: her children’s school fees, house maintenance, health costs, and Christmas expenses. Donna often feels that her hard-earned money is not used wisely. Here she is seen sending money for her eldest son's first day at university and as a Christmas gift for her parents. Little does she know that only 2 days later, her mother will suffer a near-fatal stroke because she didn't dare ask for money for her blood pressure medication. She will spend New Year's Eve in intensive care. This store, run by Filipinos for Filipinos in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, where most of the Filipino community works, offers favorable exchange rates. Expatriate remittances to the Philippines make up 10 to 15%of the country's GDP.

Caption: Tublay, Philippines. August 2019. It's the big day for Nicole. She is the first in the family to graduate from university. The whole family is mobilized around her. Her aunt helps her with her hair. Everyone will drive three hours to Baguio for the ceremony, even though only two people will be able to enter the university grounds.

Title: DONNA, technology as the only way to strengthen family relationships through a life of exile
 
Photographer: Thomas Morel-Fort

Caption: December 2024, Paris. 8 years later, the cuddly ladybird is still there (on the chair at the center). But since January, for the first time in her life, Donna has been living alone, not in a space shared with roommates or her employers. So the seven-story walk-up, the shared toilet on the landing, and the 9m² space are a small price to pay for the luxury of having a room of her own. At last, she can arrange her little haven as she pleases, filling it with as many plants as she likes. Gradually, she feels more independent and even begins to plan for the future. She dreams of bringing her son over to live with her in Paris. And even better, of securing legal residency in France, which would allow her to travel to the Philippines and finally see her family again after 12 years. But this year, that dream crumbled when her residence permit application was deemed incomplete. Now, she must start the entire process over again.

Caption: Baguio city.August 2019. Ceremony for Nicole's nursing diploma. Nicole wears the traditional graduation outfit: headdress, toga, scarf. She realizes her mother's dream of becoming a nurse. One of the great absentees of this particular day, Donna.
